To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rheological models of liver tissue with simple steatosis (fat accumulation) or steatohepatititis (fat accumulation with inflammation) are different and can be captured by different rheological models.

(1) the dominant visco-elastic behaviors associated with steatosis and inflammation in the normal liver can be captured by a simple rheological model, (2) this model can be used to predict the effects of these changes on the shear wave speed and the viscoelastic parameters measured using elastographic techniques, and (3) these results are useful for improved design of elastographic techniques to diagnose steatosis and/or steatohepatits in the liver.

the viscoelastic behavior of liver with steatosis and inflammation can be captured using a simple rheological model, and that this model can be used to predict changes in elastographic parameters due to these conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biomechanics of fatty liver disease.
the development of new mathematical models for the viscoelastic behavior of the liver.

the biomechanics of fatty liver disease, and in particular with the effects of simple steatotic and steatohepatic livers on the shear wave speed and other viscoelastic parameters that can be obtained using different elastographic modalities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the biomechanics of steatohepatitic livers are complex and not fully understood.

, while the presence of steatosis and/or steatohepatitits can be associated with changes in the shear wave speed, the magnitude and direction of these changes is not always predictable, and can vary depending on the specific rheological model that is assumed.
the shear modulus of liver tissue increases with the degree of steatosis, while the shear wave attenuation coefficient decreases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the shear wave speed in liver tissue increases as fat content increases.
the viscoelastic properties of the liver are altered by simple steatosis, steatohepatis and fibrosis.

the viscoelastic properties of steatotic liver can be modeled as a viscoelastic fluid, while the viscoelastic property of steatohepatitic liver can be modeled using the Maxwell viscoelastic fluid model.
The main takeaway from our work is that
shear wave speed is a poor indicator of the degree of fibrosis in the liver.
shear wave speed is a poor measure of fibrosis, and the effects of steatosis and inflammation on shear wave speed are small and difficult to detect.

the effects of fat accumulation on the liver's viscoelasticity can be described in terms of an increase in the tissue's shear modulus and a reduction in the tissue's loss tangent (or, equivalently, a decrease in the tissue's damping coefficient).
